summary: For children aged 5–6 extending secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing to the full 0–100 range. The goal is procedural fluency in reading and writing two-digit numerals by exploiting the regular pattern (left digit = tens, right digit = ones), targeting the persistent trouble spots: the spoken-order transposition (writing 'forty-two' as 24), decade-boundary crossings (29→30, 79→80), and keeping the 0 in decade numbers. This is numeral fluency, not yet full place-value reasoning.
misconceptions: Transposing spoken two-digit numbers (writing 'forty-two' as 24) — confusing the ones-first teens with the tens-first pattern of the rest.
Decade-boundary errors when counting/writing (after 29 saying/writing 'twenty-ten', or 39→50).
Reading a two-digit numeral as two separate digits ('four, two' for 42) rather than as forty-two.
Miswriting the 'ty' decades (writing 70 as 17, confusing seventy/seventeen).
Omitting or misplacing 0 in decade numbers (writing 40 as 4, or 'forty' as 400).

activities.title: Hear-it, build-it, place-it on a hundred square
steps: Listen to a spoken two-digit number (e.g. 'sixty-eight') and write or point to its numeral.
Place the numeral in its position on a 100-square (state whether it is a 1–100 or a 0–99 layout), then check whether it lands where that number belongs.
Build a number from tens-and-ones cards: compose 42 by taking the '40' card and placing the '2' over its zero, so the tens and ones are explicitly separated.
Work across decade boundaries: continue 28, 29, __ and 78, 79, __ , writing each numeral (30 and 80).
Do both directions: say-it → write it; show it → read it aloud; point-to-it on the grid.
activities.insight: 0–100 is one regular system, not a hundred separate facts: moving down a column the tens digit goes up while the ones digit stays the same, and moving along a row the ones digit changes. On a 0–99 square each row shares one tens digit. On a 1–100 square the decade number (10, 20, … 100) ends each row, so it is the one cell in its row with a different tens digit. Either way, each numeral means 'this far along', not just two loose digits.

activities.title: Minimal-pair contrast: -teen versus -ty
steps: Read aloud the auditory -teen/-ty pairs: 13 and 30, 14 and 40, 17 and 70 (seventeen/seventy); then the separate reading-order/transposition pair 17 and 71 (seventeen/seventy-one).
Take dictation of 'forty' then 'fourteen'; write each and compare.
Explain or show how 40 and 14 differ, e.g. with base-ten sticks: forty is 4 tens; fourteen is one ten and 4.
Say the endings clearly: contrast the spoken ones-first teens (thir-TEEN) with the spoken tens-first rest (FORTY-two), while noting both are written tens-first (13 and 42).
activities.insight: The teens 13–19 are SAID with the ones idea first (a special '-teen' word), and eleven and twelve are irregular words. All of them, like every two-digit number, are WRITTEN tens-first (11, 12, 13, 14). Numbers from 20 up are both said and written tens-first. Seeing that teens are spoken in a different order from how they are written helps keep the two patterns apart and supports moving past writing 41 for fourteen as place value develops.

activities.title: Fluency check: read, write, place, order
steps: Write the numeral for a spoken number (e.g. 'forty-two' → 42).
Read a shown numeral aloud (e.g. 68 as 'sixty-eight', not 'six, eight').
Place a numeral on a 0–100 line (e.g. position 68).
Order a short sequence across a decade boundary, e.g. fill the gaps around 29→30.
Write the number that is one more than 19 (20); write 'sixty-two' then 'twenty-six' and check they differ.
activities.insight: Reading and writing to 100 should be reliable in both directions and across decade crossings, with minimal pairs kept distinct and the zero kept in decade numbers.

checkQuestion: Watch the child read and write. First: 'Read these aloud: 13, 30, 17, 71.' Then dictate for them to write: 'forty … fourteen … sixty-two … twenty-six.' Watch the minimal pairs (13/30, 14/40, 62/26) rather than asking them about the numbers.
checkAnswer: Reads all four correctly and writes 40, 14, 62, 26 — distinguishing 13 from 30 and not transposing 62/26.
